A dual-polarization mmWave transceiver platform, taken from architecture to a fabrication-ready PCB.

This diploma thesis delivers the complete PCB design of a 28–31 GHz Time Division Duplex (TDD) transceiver platform: two AKRONIC ALTUS28TR transceiver ICs, one per polarization branch, a shared NEXUS28Z local-oscillator PLL, and two Red Pitaya STEMlab 125-14 boards providing full analog I/Q baseband access.

Every critical design decision, from power integrity to baseband interfaces and RF/LO routing, is backed by circuit-level LTspice simulation or full-wave electromagnetic extraction in RFPro.

What this work demonstrates

The hard part of a project like this is not any single block — it is keeping component selection, interface circuits, supply rails, controlled-impedance routing, digital control and simulation checks consistent with the same system assumptions, all the way from the block diagram to the routed board. The thesis crosses four engineering domains and closes the loop between them:

SYSTEM DESIGNArchitecture to implementation

Dual-branch transceiver architecture with shared frequency reference, TDD timing plan, and interface definitions carried consistently into hardware.

POWER ELECTRONICS / INTEGRITYMulti-rail power network (PDN) design

Buck + LDO power tree from a single 5 V input, ±2.5 V analog rails, ferrite-bead post-filtering, decoupling strategy, and per-rail LTspice verification down to sub-mV point-of-load ripple.

ANALOG / MIXED-SIGNALPrecision FDA interfaces

LTC6409 and ADA4927 fully differential stages designed for impedance, level and common-mode targets — verified in transient and AC domain, including non-ideal component models.

RF / EM & SOFTWAREmmWave layout, proven by full-wave EM

GCPW routing on a hybrid RO4350B stackup, with the two most sensitive structures extracted in RFPro on the real layout geometry; Python host framework closing the TDD control loop.

Application space

The 28–31 GHz range partially overlaps the 5G NR FR2 spectrum and serves high-capacity links. The board is built as a research platform with open analog baseband access:

[ FR2 ]

5G NR mmWave

Physical-layer experimentation in FR2 spectrum segments with real mmWave ICs and software TDD frame control.

[ FWA ]

Fixed Wireless Access

High-capacity fixed wireless links in the microwave/mmWave region.

[ PTP ]

Directional links with dual polarization and a common frequency reference across both branches.

[ LAB ]

The site follows the thesis structure. Chapter 04B collects the full verification campaign — power integrity, baseband interfaces, EM extraction and TDD software — in one place.

Chapter 01

Introduction & Objective

At 30 GHz the PCB is no longer a passive carrier — it is part of the circuit. Short routing segments, component pads, connector launches and vias directly affect matching and loss, so the board itself must be engineered like an RF component.

The motivation comes from the growth of mmWave communications: the 28–31 GHz range offers wide bandwidth for 5G FR2, fixed wireless access and point-to-point links. Working experimentally at these frequencies requires a hardware platform that combines real mmWave ICs with open, well-conditioned access to the baseband.

Objective

The objective is the complete transfer of a system architecture into a manufacturable PCB: component selection, interface circuits, power distribution, controlled-impedance routing, and simulation-based sign-off of the highest-risk items. The thesis deliberately stops before fabrication — the emphasis is on the layout and on documenting the critical regions with circuit-level and electromagnetic simulation, so the design package is ready for fabrication, bring-up and laboratory evaluation.

Methodology at a glance

  • System architecture: polarization branches, LO plan, baseband interface definitions and TDD control scheme.
  • Circuit design: power distribution network, FDA conditioning stages, RF front-end, LO distribution, digital control subsystem.
  • PCB layout in KiCad: six-layer hybrid RO4350B/FR-4 stackup with grounded coplanar waveguide routing on the top layer.
  • Verification: LTspice for every supply rail and both baseband interfaces; full-wave EM extraction in RFPro for the critical mmWave structures; Python framework implementing host-side TDD control.
Chapter 02

Theoretical Background

Four concepts carry the whole design: TDD operation, Zero-IF transceiver architecture, controlled-impedance transmission lines on PCB, and fully differential amplifiers at the baseband boundary.

Time Division Duplex

In TDD, transmit and receive share the same spectral channel in alternating time slots. Guard intervals between them give the RF switches and the rest of the chain time to change state — a constraint that later defines the host-side GPIO control sequence.

TDD frame · same channel, alternating slots 1 FRAME = 11 ms · SHOWN ×400 SLOWER

Zero-IF Transceivers & the LO

The ALTUS28TR follows a Zero-IF architecture: in-phase/quadrature (I/Q) baseband signals are translated directly to RF through a local oscillator, with no intermediate frequency stage. LO quality and distribution therefore become critical, which is why the platform derives both polarization branches from a single shared phase-locked loop (PLL).

mmWave PCB: Microstrip vs GCPW

At 28–31 GHz every trace is a transmission line. The design selects grounded coplanar waveguide (GCPW) for RF and LO routing: the coplanar ground with via fencing suppresses radiation and holds a better-controlled impedance in dense layout than plain microstrip.

Fully Differential Amplifiers

The Red Pitaya boards expose single-ended ports, while the ALTUS28TR requires a differential I/Q interface at a defined common-mode level. FDAs bridge the two: single-ended-to-differential conversion, level translation, and explicit common-mode control — the foundation for the baseband conditioning chains of Chapter 4.

Chapter 03

System Architecture

Two ALTUS28TR transceivers, one per polarization branch. One NEXUS28Z PLL as the shared LO source. Two Red Pitaya STEMlab 125-14 boards as the external baseband subsystem. All of it tied together with TDD switching and SPI control.

The shared frequency reference lets the two polarizations operate coherently. The final relative phase between branches also depends on LO distribution, path lengths and board tolerances — a constraint that drove the symmetric LO fan-out in the layout chapter.

Transceiver IC: ALTUS28TR

Each ALTUS28TR integrates the transmit chain (I/Q modulator, driver), the receive chain (low-noise amplifier, demodulator) and the LO path, configured over a serial peripheral interface (SPI). Its differential I/Q interface, input common-mode requirement and drive levels define the specifications of the FDA stages.

PLL / Synthesizer: NEXUS28Z

Baseband: Red Pitaya + FDA interface

The STEMlab 125-14 boards generate and acquire the analog I/Q signals. Per branch, an FDA stage adapts levels, impedance and common-mode between their single-ended ports and the transceiver's differential interface.

Chapter 04 · Sections 4.1–4.6 · Design

Circuit Design & PCB Implementation

From schematics to a routed board: power distribution, baseband conditioning, RF front-end with TDD switching, LO distribution and a six-layer hybrid stackup — designed in KiCad with hierarchical schematics and controlled-impedance rules.

SEC. 4.1Power Distribution Network

From a single 5 V input, buck converters generate the main positive IC rails; low-dropout regulators (LDOs) provide the low-noise 1.8 V PLL rail and the auxiliary 3.3 V digital rail; the FDA stages get dedicated ±2.5 V supplies. Ferrite beads and local decoupling isolate converter switching noise from each point of load.

Every rail also carries external injection pads plus jumper selection, so it can be fed and validated in isolation during bring-up.

SEC. 4.2Baseband Signal Conditioning

The transmit path uses the LTC6409: it presents a ~50 Ω load to the Red Pitaya DAC, performs single-ended-to-differential conversion, and sets the ALTUS28TR input common-mode near 0.5 V through a dedicated buffered reference. The receive path, built on the ADA4927, provides gain, DC-level translation and differential-to-single-ended conversion, driving the ADC with a ground-centered signal.

SEC. 4.3–4.4RF Front-End & LO Distribution

Each polarization branch reaches its 2.92 mm connector through a MASW-011145 single-pole double-throw (SPDT) switch implementing the TDD TX/RX changeover. The LO chain allows selection between the on-board PLL and an external source, amplifies through a gain block, and splits symmetrically toward the two ALTUS28TR devices — keeping the branch-to-branch phase relationship as deterministic as the board allows.

SEC. 4.6Hybrid Stackup & Layout Discipline

The stackup carries design intent. RO4350B occupies the outer dielectric regions where the RF/LO GCPW lines run; cost-effective S1000-2M fills the inner core for power planes and control routing. The mmWave paths stay on low-loss laminate without forcing the whole board onto RF material.

The GCPW geometry was designed for 50 Ω against the first inner ground layer (In1.Cu). The layout partitions RF, analog and digital regions, and copper zones with stitching vias enforce return-path control.

SEC. 4.5 / APP. DDigital Control & Design Workflow

An FT232H-based USB-to-SPI subsystem with TXB0108 level translation serves the three SPI targets at their native logic levels (2.6 V for the transceivers, 1.8 V for the PLL), with tri-state MISO isolation on the shared bus. The whole project is captured as hierarchical schematics in KiCad, with per-domain sub-sheets, electrical- and design-rule checks (ERC/DRC) passed, and manufacturing outputs generated as part of the flow.

Chapter 04 · Sections 4.7–4.9 · Verification

Verification & Results

Every major risk in the design was checked before declaring it ready for fabrication: all supply rails in transient and steady state, both baseband interfaces in time and frequency domain, the two most sensitive mmWave structures by full-wave EM extraction on the real layout geometry, and the TDD sequencing in software.

SEC. 4.7 · LTSPICEPower Integrity — every rail verified

Each rail was simulated with its regulator, post-filtering and a representative load profile: the 1.8 V core rail, the 2.6 V RF rail feeding both transceivers, and the +2.5 V / −2.5 V FDA rails, including startup behavior of the negative supply. The frequency-domain output impedance of the heavily loaded 2.6 V rail was extracted separately to confirm the decoupling network holds across the relevant band.

SEC. 4.7.6–4.7.8 · LTSPICEBaseband Interfaces — time & frequency domain

The TX interface was simulated with the full external network: the LTC6409 stage, the output common-mode (VOCM) bias, split termination, series damping and a simplified transceiver-side continuation, including non-ideal resistor models and the PCB launch network in the AC analysis. Input impedance seen by the Red Pitaya source and differential output impedance were both extracted.

The RX interface was excited by the differential receiver-buffer model and checked at the ADC-side node in transient and AC domain. The buffered 0.5 V common-mode reference network was verified to settle correctly.

SEC. 4.9 · RFPROElectromagnetic Verification on the Real Layout

Closed-form transmission-line estimates stop being reliable where the geometry gets complex. The two highest-risk regions were therefore exported from the actual KiCad layout and solved with full-wave EM simulation in RFPro.

The implemented stackup was recreated layer by layer in the EM environment, ground–signal–ground (GSG) ports were placed at the physical launch locations, the mesh was refined around signal paths and via regions, and the exported S-parameter files were evaluated in an N-port circuit testbench.

LO transition. The final fan-out from the splitter toward the two transceivers, including the single vertical layer transition kept in the LO path:

RF/TDD switch region. The dense multi-port area around the MASW-011145 SPDT — connector transition, local ground shape and adjacent branches interacting in a few square millimeters. This is deliberately the hardest test in the thesis:

SEC. 4.8 / APP. A–C · PYTHONTDD Software Control — closing the loop

A modular Python framework on the host configures both Red Pitaya boards, defines the TDD time slots and guard intervals, and drives the GPIO signals that switch the RF front-end. The simulated frame sequencing shows baseband activity, GPIO switch control, frame states and the resulting power envelope lining up as designed, and the framework generates representative waveform classes whose power spectral densities were verified.

Chapter 05

Conclusions & Outlook

The thesis delivers a routed, DRC-clean, simulation-verified PCB design package for a dual-polarization TDD transceiver at 28–31 GHz — with the power network, both baseband interfaces and the critical mmWave structures signed off by simulation before fabrication.

What the work established

  • The genuinely hard problem is the consistent transfer from architecture to PCB: components, interfaces, supplies, routing and verification all had to obey the same system assumptions.
  • The hybrid stackup is an engineering decision with a cost dimension: RO4350B only where the mmWave paths need it, standard laminate everywhere else.
  • The LO path proved controllable (short, one layer transition, <0.1 dB insertion loss), while the SPDT switch region is the tightest part of the RF layout — identified, quantified, and flagged as the first item to revisit in a revision B.
  • PDN and baseband interfaces met their design targets in simulation: sub-mV point-of-load ripple on all rails, ~50 Ω / 1.6 Vpp on TX, 2 Vpp ground-centered on RX.

Limitations

The board was not fabricated within the thesis timeline, so the results describe expected pre-manufacturing behavior. EM verification is local (LO transition and RF/TDD switch region) rather than full-board, and connector launch behavior, soldering, package tolerances and manufacturing spread remain outside the simulated results. Identifying exactly where simulation stops and measurement must begin is part of the engineering.

Next steps

  • Fabrication, assembly and bring-up, using the external injection pads designed in for isolated rail validation.
  • Laboratory RF measurements and correlation against the EM extractions.
  • Geometry revision around the SPDT switch in rev. B.
  • Physical-layer experiments with the Python TDD framework across both polarizations.
